title: How to build an AI training dataset from the web, step by step
summary: Build an AI training dataset from the web in seven steps: scope, source, collect, clean, label, format as JSONL and validate, with a tested Firecrawl pipeline.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR**


- **An AI training dataset is a set of examples in one fixed shape** that a model learns from, such as question and answer pairs, labeled text or plain documents. OpenAI accepts a fine-tuning file with as few as **10 examples** and suggests starting with **50 well-written ones** .
- **Training data comes from five places:** open datasets, web crawl archives, the live web, licensed providers and synthetic examples. Common Crawl's October 2026 archive alone holds **2.16 billion pages** , but a domain fine-tuning set needs a few thousand pages chosen on purpose.
- **Building one from the web takes seven steps:** scope, source, collect, clean and dedupe, label, format as **JSONL** and validate. Most broken datasets come from a skipped step, not a bad source.
- **Deduplication and grounding decide the quality.** The CuraWeb corpus combined n-gram and semantic deduplication to reach **2 trillion tokens** , and a 3B model trained on it scored **1.8% higher** on average than the baselines it was compared with. Check every model-written label against a sentence on its source page.
- **Split by source website, not by row.** Near-duplicate pages from one site otherwise land in both the training and validation files and inflate the evaluation score.
- **Firecrawl is a great fit for building AI training datasets from the web.** One API key covers sourcing and collection: Firecrawl /search finds pages and PDFs, Firecrawl /scrape and Firecrawl /crawl turn them into clean Markdown or schema-shaped JSON (JavaScript-rendered pages included), and Firecrawl Alexandria adds licensed and curated data from **400+ sources** (some providers need an org admin to accept their terms first). Licensed data is a growing source too, with **91 publicly announced AI content licensing deals** by June 2026.
- **If you need a custom dataset built for you,**[contact the Firecrawl team](https://www.firecrawl.dev/contact-sales) .


---


## What is an AI training dataset?


An AI training dataset is a collection of examples, all in the same structure, that a model learns patterns from. A chat model learns from prompt and response pairs, a classifier learns from text with labels, and a base model learns from large amounts of plain documents. Each example should be accurate, on topic and traceable to where it came from.


The shape of the dataset follows from what you want the model to do:


Dataset type One record looks like Used for


Pretraining corpus A document's text, with source and date Teaching a base model language and facts


Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) A user message and the ideal assistant reply Teaching a chat model a task, tone or domain


Preference pairs One prompt with a preferred and a rejected reply Tuning which answers a model favors


Classification set A piece of text and its label Routing, tagging, moderation, sentiment


Evaluation set A held-out prompt and its expected answer Measuring whether training helped


Fine-tuning sets can be small.[OpenAI's supervised fine-tuning guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/supervised-fine-tuning) sets the minimum at 10 examples, sees improvements from 50 to 100, and recommends starting with 50 well-crafted demonstrations. The[Unsloth datasets guide](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/datasets-guide) suggests at least 100 rows and prefers more than 1,000. Pretraining corpora are far bigger, and CuraWeb, a 2026 English corpus built from Common Crawl, holds 2 trillion tokens.


If you are deciding whether a model needs training at all, our comparison of[training data, retrieved data and live web data](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/training-vs-retrieved-vs-live-web-data) covers when fine-tuning helps and when retrieval is the better fix.


## Where does AI training data come from?


AI training data comes from five places: pages you collect from the live web with Firecrawl, open datasets that someone already published, web crawl archives such as Common Crawl, licensed data from providers, and synthetic examples a model writes. Most teams combine two or three, because each source covers a gap the others leave.


Source What you get How fresh Best for


Live web with Firecrawl /search and /scrape Pages you pick, as Markdown or JSON Fetched when you run it Domain datasets, niche topics, recent facts


Open datasets (Hugging Face Hub, Kaggle) Ready-made records with a dataset card Fixed at publication Common tasks someone already collected


Web crawl archives (Common Crawl) Raw page captures in WARC files Monthly snapshots Pretraining at very large scale


Licensed providers through Firecrawl Alexandria (400+ sources) Structured records with source and license fields Current at call time Data that comes from an official or paid source


Synthetic data from a model Examples a model generates from a prompt As fresh as the model Filling gaps once you have real seed data


[Common Crawl's October 2026 archive](https://commoncrawl.org/blog/october-2026-crawl-archive-now-available) , published October 21, holds 2.16 billion pages (371 TiB of uncompressed content) from 34.3 million registered domains, a scale that suits pretraining a base model. A fine-tuning set about one domain needs a few thousand pages chosen on purpose, which is what search and scraping give you.


Licensed data is a growing source as well. The Media & the Machine tracker counted[91 publicly announced AI content licensing deals](https://mediaandthemachine.substack.com/p/ai-content-licensing-deals-june-2026) by June 2026, and it projects that deals for ongoing access to content will reach 34 in 2026, up from 18 in 2025.

## How do you build an AI training dataset from the web, step by step?


Building an AI training dataset from the web takes seven steps: scope the task, find sources, collect the pages, clean and deduplicate the text, label each example, write it in a training format such as JSONL, and validate the result. Firecrawl handles the source and collect steps, and returns structured records that make the rest short.


Step What you do Firecrawl piece


1. Scope Decide the task, the record shape and the target count Not needed


2. Source Find pages, papers, PDFs or provider data on the topic Firecrawl /search, Firecrawl Alexandria, Firecrawl indexes


3. Collect Turn each page into clean text or JSON Firecrawl /scrape, Firecrawl /crawl, PDF parsing


4. Clean and dedupe Drop boilerplate, near-duplicates and off-topic records` only_main_content` strips navigation and footers


5. Label Attach the answer, class or score to each example JSON schema extraction with a prompt


6. Format Write JSONL and split into train and validation files Not needed


7. Validate Check structure, grounding, balance and leakage Source URL on every record


### How do you scope a training dataset?


Scoping means writing down three things before collecting anything: the task the model should learn, what one record looks like, and how many you need. "Answer homeowner questions about heat pumps in two sentences, from public guidance" is a scope. "Collect heat pump data" is not, because it gives you no way to say which pages belong.


Write a sample record by hand first. If you can't write five good examples yourself, a model can't learn the task from five thousand scraped ones.


### How do you clean and deduplicate web data?


Cleaning removes everything on a page that isn't the content, such as menus, cookie banners, footers, ads and related-post lists. Firecrawl's` only_main_content` option does most of this at collection time. After that, drop records that are too short, off topic or in the wrong language.


Web data needs deduplication because the same paragraph shows up on many sites. Run an exact pass that hashes normalized text, then a near-duplicate pass that compares word shingles or embeddings. The CuraWeb paper ([arXiv, June 29, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22662) ) combined n-gram and semantic deduplication with quality filtering to build a 2 trillion token English corpus from Common Crawl, and a 3B model trained on it scored 1.8% higher on average than the baselines it was compared with.


### How do you label web data for training?


Labeling attaches the target to each example, whether that is the ideal answer, a class or a score. For question and answer data, a model can draft the pairs from the page itself, which is what Firecrawl /scrape does when you give it a JSON schema. Ask for a supporting quote with every label, then check that the quote appears on the page. That check is cheap and it catches answers that drift away from the source.


Do that check in code rather than trusting the prompt. In[Lenny's Newsletter](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/how-to-do-ai-analysis-you-can-actually) , user researcher[Caitlin Sullivan](https://www.linkedin.com/in/caitlindsullivan/) reports that, over 2,000 hours spent testing AI analysis workflows, she saw every major model still produce invented quotes, plus "Frankenstein" quotes stitched together from several sources. She also found that length caps such as "12 words or fewer" almost always produce those mash-ups, so ask for a full sentence instead. Her explanation of why it happens applies to model-written training labels too:


> LLMs don't retrieve quotes like a search engine; they generate text that's statistically likely given the context.


*Caitlin Sullivan, Lenny's Newsletter, February 2026*


Labels that need judgment, such as tone or the right answer to a hard question, still need a person. Our[guide to custom instruction datasets](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/custom-instruction-datasets-llm-fine-tuning) covers writing instruction pairs by hand and with a model.


### What format should a training dataset use?


JSONL, short for JSON Lines, is the standard format for fine-tuning data. Each line holds one complete JSON object, so a file can be streamed, appended to and split without parsing the whole thing. OpenAI's fine-tuning API requires JSONL with at least 10 lines, and the Hugging Face` datasets` library loads it directly. Chat data goes in a` messages` list with` user` and` assistant` turns.


Keep a` metadata` object on each line with the source URL, the fetch time and anything else you might filter on later. Training code ignores it, and it is how you trace a bad example back to the page it came from.


### How do you validate a dataset before training?


Validation checks that every line parses, has the right roles and non-empty content, and still matches its source. It also checks the split. Splitting by source website keeps near-identical examples from one site out of both files at once, which would otherwise inflate your evaluation score.


## How does Firecrawl help you build training datasets?


Firecrawl, the context API for AI agents, is a great fit for building training datasets from the web because it covers the steps where most of the work sits. Firecrawl /search finds sources across the web and Firecrawl's own indexes. Firecrawl /scrape, Firecrawl /crawl and PDF parsing turn those sources into clean Markdown or structured JSON. Firecrawl Alexandria adds licensed and curated provider data through the same API key.


Here is what that removes from a dataset pipeline:


- **Boilerplate cleanup.** The` only_main_content` option drops navigation, headers and footers at collection time, so each record starts close to the page's actual content.
- **Pages that need a browser.** Firecrawl renders JavaScript-heavy pages and reads PDFs through the same scrape call, so your sources aren't limited to static HTML.
- **Parsing scraped text into records.** A JSON schema and a prompt return the fields you define, such as a question, an answer and a supporting quote from the page.
- **Lost provenance.** Every result carries its source URL in` metadata` , plus the page title when the page has one, which the grounding and split checks rely on.
- **Rebuilding for scale.** Firecrawl /crawl collects a whole site, and batch scrape runs the same extraction across thousands of URLs as one job.


The same pieces serve larger training work too. Firecrawl's[AI training use case page](https://www.firecrawl.dev/use-cases/ai-training) covers web data for pre-training, search inside reinforcement learning rollouts, and evals checked against real pages.


Minimal, an AI customer support platform for e-commerce brands, processes nearly six million storefront pages a month through Firecrawl, turning live product and policy content into data its AI support agents answer from, as described in[Minimal's customer story](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/how-minimal-builds-ai-support-agents-with-firecrawl) .


> Storefronts come to us in every shape imaginable, and no matter the complexity, Firecrawl turns each one into clean, structured data our AI support agents can answer from.


*Niek Hogenboom, Co-Founder, Minimal*

## How does Firecrawl Alexandria add licensed data to a training dataset?


Firecrawl Alexandria gives AI agents and scripts structured data from 400+ official and licensed sources through the same Firecrawl API key, MCP server and CLI they use for search and scraping. Providers are paid under agreement when agents pull their data, and records arrive with their source fields, so a training example can carry where it came from and under what license. Some providers need an org admin to accept their terms in the Firecrawl dashboard before the first call.


Finding a tool is free. Each tool shows its price in Firecrawl credits before you call it, and you pay with Firecrawl credits at that price with no per-vendor minimum. Firecrawl's own indexes sit in the same catalog:


- **Research Index:** about 43 million paper abstracts across PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv and arXiv, with tools to read passages and find related papers.
- **Developer Index:** issues, merged pull requests and READMEs from public code repositories, plus curated documentation sites.
- **Government Index:** US federal, state and local statutes, regulations, codes and court opinions.


Firecrawl Alexandria has already supplied a training set. Our walkthrough on[fine-tuning Laya on a Mac](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/fine-tune-laya) built 2,980 query and result pairs from the Developer Index for about 600 Firecrawl credits.


These are the dataset jobs we ran through Firecrawl Alexandria on October 27, 2026:


Dataset job Firecrawl Alexandria provider and capability


Check whether a dataset already exists, and its license[Hugging Face](https://www.firecrawl.dev/alexandria/huggingface-co)` hub/datasets`


Pull reference text with its license and revision[Wikipedia](https://www.firecrawl.dev/alexandria/wikipedia)` articles/structured-contents`


Find paper abstracts on a topic[Research Index](https://www.firecrawl.dev/alexandria/firecrawl-research-index)` search` ,` inspect`


Find code examples, docs and issues[Developer Index](https://www.firecrawl.dev/alexandria/firecrawl-developer-index)` search`


This script runs the first three. It checks the Hugging Face Hub for existing heat pump datasets, adds the current Wikipedia article with its license, and adds paper abstracts from the Research Index, skipping abstracts that come back shortened:


```text
import   json  ,   os
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


client   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


def   call  (  provider  ,   capability  ,   **  options  ):
result   =   client  .  scrape  (
alexandria  =  {  "provider"  : provider,   "capability"  : capability,   "options"  : options}
).  alexandria  [  0  ]
if   result  .  error  :
raise   RuntimeError  (result.error)
return   result  .  data  ,   result  .  credits_cost


# Check what already exists before building anything
hub  ,   hub_cost   =   call  (  "huggingface-co"  ,   "hub/datasets"  , search  =  "heat-pump"  , limit  =  10  )
print  (  f  "Hugging Face datasets matching 'heat-pump':   {  hub[  'count'  ]  }  "  )


docs   =   []


# Licensed reference text: the current Wikipedia revision, with its license attached
articles  ,   wiki_cost   =   call  (
"wikipedia"  ,   "articles/structured-contents"  , name  =  "Heat pump"  ,
fields  =  [  "name"  ,   "abstract"  ,   "url"  ,   "license"  ,   "version.identifier"  ,   "date_modified"  ],
)
for   article   in   articles  :
docs  .  append  ({
"text"  : article[  "abstract"  ],
"source"  : article[  "url"  ],
"license"  : article[  "license"  ][  0  ][  "identifier"  ],
"revision"  : article[  "version"  ][  "identifier"  ],
})


# Paper abstracts from the Firecrawl Research Index
papers  ,   research_cost   =   call  (
"firecrawl-research-index"  ,   "search"  ,
query  =  "air source heat pump performance in cold climates"  , k  =  10  ,   **  {  "from"  :   "2023-01-01"  },
)
truncated   =   0
for   paper   in   papers  [  "results"  ]:
if   paper  [  "abstract"  ].  endswith  (  "…"  ):
truncated   +=   1
continue
docs  .  append  ({
"text"  :   f  "  {  paper[  'title'  ]  }  \n\n  {  paper[  'abstract'  ]  }  "  ,
"source"  : paper[  "primaryId"  ],
"license"  :   None  ,
"revision"  :   None  ,
})


with   open  (  "heat_pump_docs.jsonl"  ,   "w"  )   as   f  :
for   doc   in   docs  :
f  .  write  (json.  dumps  (doc, ensure_ascii  =  False  )   +   "\n"  )


print  (json.  dumps  ({
"documents"  :   len  (docs),
"skipped_truncated_abstracts"  : truncated,
"licenses"  :   sorted  ({d[  "license"  ]   for   d   in   docs   if   d[  "license"  ]}),
"credits"  : {  "hugging_face"  : hub_cost,   "wikipedia"  : wiki_cost,   "research_index"  : research_cost},
}))
```


Output from the run:


```text
Hugging Face datasets matching 'heat-pump': 0
{"documents": 5, "skipped_truncated_abstracts": 6, "licenses": ["CC-BY-SA-4.0"], "credits": {"hugging_face": 5, "wikipedia": 1, "research_index": 0}}
```


No dataset ID on the Hub matched "heat-pump", which is the signal to build one. The Wikipedia record carries the license` CC-BY-SA-4.0` and a revision ID, and Firecrawl Alexandria labels Wikipedia results "Retrieved through Wikimedia Enterprise." Six of the ten paper abstracts came back shortened with an ellipsis, so the script left them out instead of training on cut-off text.

## How do you find training data sources with Firecrawl /search?


Firecrawl /search takes a query and returns ranked web results, and it can scrape each result in the same call. For dataset work, its category filters narrow results to one source type, such as PDFs, the Firecrawl Developer Index, the Firecrawl Government Index or academic sites.


[Firecrawl /search](https://www.firecrawl.dev/search) sets those filters with the` categories` parameter:` pdf` ,` developer` ,` gov` and` research` . A few other options matter when you collect training data:


- **` scrape_options`** returns each result's Markdown or JSON with the search, so one call both finds and collects a page.
- **` tbs`** limits results by date (` qdr:m` for the past month), which keeps a dataset current.
- **` site:`** inside the query restricts results to one domain, such as an official documentation site.
- **` sources: \["news"\]`** returns news articles instead of web pages.


A search costs 2 Firecrawl credits per 10 results, and each scraped result adds the cost of a scrape.


## How do you turn web pages into training records with Firecrawl /scrape?


Firecrawl /scrape turns a URL into Markdown, HTML or structured JSON. With a JSON schema and a prompt, it returns exactly the fields you define, so a page comes back as training records instead of text you still have to parse.


The script below runs[Firecrawl /scrape](https://www.firecrawl.dev/scrape) through the search call's` scrape_options` and covers pipeline steps 2 to 7. It searches three heat pump queries, asks for up to five question and answer pairs per page with a supporting sentence quoted from the page, keeps only pairs whose quote appears in the page text, removes exact and near-duplicate questions, and writes chat-format JSONL split by website:


```text
import   hashlib  ,   json  ,   os  ,   re
from   datetime   import   datetime  ,   timezone
from   urllib  .  parse   import   urlsplit
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl
from   firecrawl  .  v2  .  types   import   ScrapeOptions


client   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


QUERIES   =   [
"how do air source heat pumps work in cold weather"  ,
"heat pump sizing and installation guide for homes"  ,
"heat pump vs furnace running costs explained"  ,
]
QA_SCHEMA   =   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"qa_pairs"  :   {
"type"  :   "array"  ,
"items"  :   {
"type"  :   "object"  ,
"properties"  :   {
"question"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  },
"answer"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  },
"evidence"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  },
"difficulty"  :   {  "type"  :   "string"  ,   "enum"  :   [  "beginner"  ,   "intermediate"  ,   "advanced"  ]  },
},
"required"  :   [  "question"  ,   "answer"  ,   "evidence"  ,   "difficulty"  ]  ,
},
}
},
"required"  :   [  "qa_pairs"  ]  ,
}
PROMPT   =   (
"Write up to 5 questions a homeowner might ask that this page answers, each with a short answer. "
"In evidence, copy one sentence from the page, word for word, that supports the answer."
)


def   norm  (  text  ):
text   =   re  .  sub  (  r  "\]\([  ^  )]  *  \)  |  https  ?  ://  \S  +  "  ,   " "  , text.  lower  ())
return   " "  .  join  (re.  sub  (  r  "[  ^  a-z0-9%$]  +  "  ,   " "  , text).  split  ())


def   shingles  (  text  ,   n  =  3  ):
words   =   norm  (text).  split  ()
return   {  " "  .  join  (words[i:i   +   n])   for   i   in   range  (  max  (  1  ,   len  (words)   -   n   +   1  ))}


# 1. Source and 2. collect: one search call per query returns pages already extracted with the schema
pages  ,   seen_urls   =   []  ,   set  ()
for   query   in   QUERIES  :
results   =   client  .  search  (
query,
limit  =  5  ,
scrape_options  =  ScrapeOptions  (
formats  =  [  "markdown"  , {  "type"  :   "json"  ,   "schema"  : QA_SCHEMA,   "prompt"  : PROMPT}],
only_main_content  =  True  ,
),
)
for   doc   in   results  .  web   or   []  :
if   not   getattr  (doc,   "json"  ,   None  )   or   not   getattr  (doc,   "markdown"  ,   None  ):
continue
key   =   doc  .  metadata  .  url  .  split  (  "#"  )  [  0  ]  .  rstrip  (  "/"  )
if   key   in   seen_urls  :
continue
seen_urls  .  add  (key)
pages  .  append  (doc)


# 3. Clean, 4. dedupe and 5. label
fetched_at   =   datetime  .  now  (timezone.utc).  isoformat  (timespec  =  "seconds"  )
records  ,   seen_questions  ,   kept_shingles   =   []  ,   set  (),   []
stats   =   {  "pages"  :   len  (pages),   "extracted"  :   0  ,   "ungrounded"  :   0  ,   "duplicates"  :   0  }
for   doc   in   pages  :
page_text   =   norm  (doc.markdown)
for   qa   in   doc  .  json  .  get  (  "qa_pairs"  , []):
stats  [  "extracted"  ]   +=   1
question  ,   answer  ,   evidence   =   (qa  .  get  (k,   ""  ).  strip  ()   for   k   in   (  "question"  ,   "answer"  ,   "evidence"  ))
if   not   question   or   len  (answer)   <   20   or   len  (evidence)   <   20   or   norm  (evidence)   not   in   page_text  :
stats  [  "ungrounded"  ]   +=   1
continue
qhash   =   hashlib  .  sha1  (  norm  (question).  encode  ()).  hexdigest  ()
qsh   =   shingles  (question)
if   qhash   in   seen_questions   or   any  (  len  (qsh   &   s)   /   len  (qsh   |   s)   >   0.6   for   s   in   kept_shingles):
stats  [  "duplicates"  ]   +=   1
continue
seen_questions  .  add  (qhash)
kept_shingles  .  append  (qsh)
records  .  append  ({
"messages"  : [
{  "role"  :   "user"  ,   "content"  : question},
{  "role"  :   "assistant"  ,   "content"  : answer},
],
"metadata"  : {
"source_url"  : doc.metadata.url,
"source_title"  :   " "  .  join  ((doc.metadata.title   or   ""  ).  split  ()),
"evidence"  : evidence,
"difficulty"  : qa.  get  (  "difficulty"  ),
"fetched_at"  : fetched_at,
},
})


# 6. Format as JSONL, split by source domain so one site never lands in both files
def   split_for  (  url  ):
domain   =   urlsplit  (url).  netloc
return   "val"   if   int  (hashlib.  md5  (domain.  encode  ()).  hexdigest  (),   16  )   %   5   ==   0   else   "train"


files   =   {  name  :   open  (  f  "heat_pump_  {  name  }  .jsonl"  ,   "w"  )   for   name   in   (  "train"  ,   "val"  )  }
for   record   in   records  :
files  [  split_for  (record[  "metadata"  ][  "source_url"  ])].  write  (json.  dumps  (record)   +   "\n"  )
for   f   in   files  .  values  ():
f  .  close  ()


# 7. Validate what landed on disk
counts   =   {}
for   name   in   files  :
with   open  (  f  "heat_pump_  {  name  }  .jsonl"  )   as   f  :
rows   =   [json  .  loads  (line)   for   line   in   f]
assert   all  ([m[  "role"  ]   for   m   in   r[  "messages"  ]]   ==   [  "user"  ,   "assistant"  ]   for   r   in   rows)
assert   all  (r[  "messages"  ][  1  ][  "content"  ]   and   r[  "metadata"  ][  "source_url"  ]   for   r   in   rows)
counts  [  name  ]   =   len  (rows)
stats  .  update  (kept  =  len  (records),   **  counts, domains  =  len  ({  urlsplit  (r[  "metadata"  ][  "source_url"  ]).netloc   for   r   in   records}))
print  (json.  dumps  (stats))
```

A few things to know about the run:


- **PDF results cost more.** Twelve web pages came to 5 Firecrawl credits each (1 for the scrape, 4 for JSON), the three searches to 6, and one result was a PDF sizing guide billed per page for 66 Firecrawl credits.
- **Normalize before you compare.** Page Markdown keeps link URLs and symbols such as ® inside sentences, so the` norm` function strips links and punctuation from both the quote and the page before matching.
- **The split is uneven at this size.** With 10 websites, hashing domains put 4 sites in validation and 6 in training. At a few hundred domains the split settles close to 80/20.
- **Pairs vary between runs.** The model writing the pairs words them a little differently each time, so earlier runs of the same script kept 56, 58 and 60 records. Keep the queries fixed and save the output you validated.
- **Scale with Firecrawl batch scrape.** When you already have a list of thousands of URLs,` client.batch_scrape(urls, formats=\[...\])` runs the same JSON extraction across all of them as one job.


## How do you get training data out of PDFs with Firecrawl?


A lot of the world's important information is buried in PDFs, including research papers, government reports, standards, manuals and spec sheets, and none of it is in a page's HTML. Firecrawl reads PDFs through the same Firecrawl /scrape call, and Firecrawl /parse takes a local file or a document that isn't online.


The engine underneath is[Fire-PDF](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/fire-pdf-launch) , built in Rust and one of the fastest PDF parsers in the world. It runs on[pdf-inspector](https://github.com/firecrawl/pdf-inspector) , Firecrawl's open-source Rust PDF library and a developer favorite with more than 19,000 GitHub stars. In pdf-inspector's[published benchmark](https://github.com/firecrawl/pdf-inspector#benchmark) on 200 PDFs, refreshed July 31, 2026, it parsed the full set in 0.47 seconds and had the highest overall, reading order and table scores of the five local engines tested.


This script finds a report with` categories=\["pdf"\]` , reads its first 25 pages, and turns each section into a record while dropping the front matter:


```text
import   json  ,   os  ,   re
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


client   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


# Find reports published as PDFs
hits   =   client  .  search  (  "DOE cold climate heat pump challenge field validation results"  , categories  =  [  "pdf"  ], limit  =  3  )
pdf_url   =   next  (hit.url   for   hit   in   hits.web   if   hit.url.  lower  ().  endswith  (  ".pdf"  ))


# Read the first 25 pages as Markdown
doc   =   client  .  scrape  (pdf_url, formats  =  [  "markdown"  ], parsers  =  [{  "type"  :   "pdf"  ,   "mode"  :   "auto"  ,   "max_pages"  :   25  }])


# Split on headings so each record is one section, and drop front matter
FRONT_MATTER   =   re  .  compile  (  r  "disclaimer  |  operated by  |  contents  |  acknowledg  |  acronyms  |  printed in  |  ^  figures  $  |  ^  tables  $  "  , re.I)
records   =   []
for   section   in   re  .  split  (  r  "\n  (?=  #  {1,6}   )  "  , doc.markdown):
heading   =   re  .  sub  (  r  "<[  ^  >]  +  >  |  ^  #  +  \s  *  "  ,   ""  , section.  strip  ().  splitlines  ()[  0  ])
if   len  (section.  split  ())   <   60   or   FRONT_MATTER  .  search  (heading):
continue
records  .  append  ({  "text"  : section.  strip  (),   "source"  : pdf_url,   "section"  : heading})
with   open  (  "heat_pump_pdf_sections.jsonl"  ,   "w"  )   as   f  :
for   record   in   records  :
f  .  write  (json.  dumps  (record)   +   "\n"  )


print  (json.  dumps  ({
"pdf"  : pdf_url,
"pages"  : doc.metadata.num_pages,
"credits"  : doc.metadata.credits_used,
"sections_kept"  :   len  (records),
"first_sections"  : [r[  "section"  ]   for   r   in   records[:  4  ]],
}))
```


Output from the run:


```text
{  "pdf"  :   "https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-37127.pdf"  ,   "pages"  :   25  ,   "credits"  :   25  ,   "sections_kept"  :   10  ,   "first_sections"  :   [  "Performance Results from DOE Cold Climate Heat Pump Challenge Field Validation"  ,   "Executive Summary"  ,   "1.0 Introduction"  ,   "1.1 Challenge Participants"  ]}
```


The PDF came to 25 Firecrawl credits, 1 per page, plus 2 Firecrawl credits for the search. The executive summary alone came back as 2,632 words, so split long sections into chunks that fit your model's context length before training. For a PDF on your own disk,` client.parse("report.pdf")` returns the same Markdown through[Firecrawl /parse](https://www.firecrawl.dev/parse) .


## How do you collect a whole site with Firecrawl /crawl?


Firecrawl /crawl follows links from a starting URL and scrapes every page it reaches, up to a limit you set. It suits sources where one site holds the whole topic, such as a documentation site, a help center or a public program's guidance pages, and path filters keep it to the part of the site you want.


The NYS Clean Heat site publishes heat pump guidance in English and Chinese. This[Firecrawl /crawl](https://www.firecrawl.dev/crawl) job keeps the English pages and skips PDFs, which get their own section in this post:


```text
import   os
from   firecrawl   import   Firecrawl


client   =   Firecrawl  (api_key  =  os.environ[  "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY"  ])


job   =   client  .  crawl  (
"https://cleanheat.ny.gov"  ,
limit  =  15  ,
exclude_paths  =  [  "^/zh-CN/.*"  ,   ".*\\.pdf$"  ],
scrape_options  =  {  "formats"  : [  "markdown"  ],   "only_main_content"  :   True  },
)
print  (job.status,   f  "  {  job.completed  }   pages,   {  job.credits_used  }   credits"  )
for   page   in   job  .  data  [:  5  ]:
print  (page.metadata.url,   len  (page.markdown.  split  ()),   "words"  )
```


Output from the run:


```text
completed 15 pages, 15 credits
https://cleanheat.ny.gov/how-they-work/ 436 words
https://cleanheat.ny.gov/compare-your-options/ 191 words
https://cleanheat.ny.gov/financing-options/ 250 words
https://cleanheat.ny.gov/find-available-rebates/ 360 words
https://cleanheat.ny.gov/what-to-expect/ 349 words
```


Crawled pages take the same` scrape_options` as a single scrape, so passing the JSON schema from the Firecrawl /scrape pipeline turns a whole site into question and answer records.

## What mistakes break AI training datasets built from the web?


The mistakes that break AI training datasets built from the web are usually skipped steps: no written scope, boilerplate left in, duplicates, unchecked labels, row-level splits, missing source URLs and truncated text. Each one is cheap to catch before a training run and expensive to find after it.


What each one looks like:


1. **No written scope.** Without a sample record and a target count, the dataset drifts toward whatever the search returned first.
2. **Boilerplate left in.** Cookie banners, menus and "related posts" lists become training text unless you collect only the main content.
3. **Duplicates across sites.** Syndicated articles and copied documentation repeat the same passage many times, which skews what the model learns.
4. **Labels nobody checked.** Model-drafted answers need a grounding check against the source and a human read of a sample.
5. **Row-level splits.** Splitting by row instead of by source puts near-identical examples in both training and validation files.
6. **Missing provenance.** Without a source URL and fetch time on each record, you can't trace or remove a bad example later.
7. **Truncated text.** Shortened abstracts, cut-off pages and over-long sections teach the model incomplete patterns. Filter and chunk them.


For preparing data you already hold, our[AI data preparation guide](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/ai-data-preparation) covers transformation and quality checks in more depth, and the guide to[data acquisition tools](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/data-acquisition-tools) compares ways to collect it.
